title: Matplotlib Multiple Plots and Subplots
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and core concepts of Matplotlib Multiple Plots and Subplots.
Select suitable Python structures or library operations for the task.
Trace the effect of each operation on the data or figure.
Validate results and interpret output accurately.
Identify limitations, edge cases and maintainability considerations.

understand.concept: A Matplotlib figure can contain multiple Axes objects arranged in a grid. plt.subplots creates the figure and axes together; each Axes owns its own plotting methods, title and labels. Shared axes and constrained layout can improve comparisons and reduce overlapping labels.
understand.whyItMatters: Subplots allow related views to be compared in one figure while keeping each chart focused.
understand.analogy: Choose the data structure or chart that matches the information being represented; visual similarity does not mean two structures have identical behavior.
understand.summary: Matplotlib Multiple Plots and Subplots adds a focused capability to the Python curriculum.

explain.narrative: Read the concept, run each example in order, inspect the returned values and figure objects, and compare the result with the stated expectation. The examples use deterministic data and a non-interactive Matplotlib backend so they can be validated in automation.

examples.title: Create two side-by-side axes
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
print(axes.size)
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: A 1-by-2 grid contains two Axes objects.

examples.title: Plot different data on each axes
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
axes[0].plot([1, 2], [2, 3])
axes[1].bar(['A', 'B'], [4, 5])
print(len(axes[0].lines), len(axes[1].patches))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: Each axes can display a different chart type.

examples.title: Set subplot titles
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
axes[0].set_title('Sales')
axes[1].set_title('Costs')
print([a.get_title() for a in axes])
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: Each axes has its own title.

examples.title: Share an x-axis
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True)
print(axes[0].get_shared_x_axes().joined(axes[0], axes[1]))
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: sharex links x-axis navigation and scale across the subplot axes.

examples.title: Export a multi-plot figure
examples.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from io import BytesIO
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, constrained_layout=True)
for ax in axes: ax.plot([1, 2], [2, 4])
buf = BytesIO(); fig.savefig(buf, format='png')
print(buf.getvalue()[:4] == b'\x89PNG')
plt.close(fig)
examples.explanation: A figure containing multiple axes can be exported as one image.
